newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Three letter bombs found at United Nations.
newsitem.headline: Three letter bombs found at United Nations.

text.p: Three letter bombs were found at the United Nations on Monday, all addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat, U.N. officials said. No one was injured.

The New York police bomb squad was called in to dismantle the third device late on Monday following a search of undelivered mail throughout the building. An estimated 20,000 pieces of mail reach the United Nations daily.
Spokesman Fred Eckhard said the third letter, found on Monday evening, was "identical to the other two" and also addressed to Al-Hayat.
"Security and regular mailroom personnel are combing the mail all night long," he added.

Security sources would not say where the third letter had been discovered but the suspicious envelope was among those taken to the General Assembly area where an electronic scanner, usually used to screen tourists, was available, in addition to the one in the main basement mailroom.
Earlier on Monday a bomb exploded at the London headquarters of the same newspaper, wounding two security guards. Four more suspected devices were subsequently found there, British police said.

In New York, the letter bombs were contained in greeting card-sized envelopes. The first was found about 11 a.m., in a second flood messenger room, about 15 minutes before it would have been delivered, Eckhard said. The second one was discovered in the basement mail room several hours later.

It was addressed to the Al-Hayat's bureau, not to any specific individual. U.N. security was on the lookout for mail addressed to Al-Hayat after its U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed them of the London incident. The second bomb was discovered in the basement.
After the first suspicious envelope was found, parts of two floors of the 38-floor complex were closed off and part of the press area evacuated.

The letters were similar to those mailed earlier this month to the same Saudi Arabian-owned newspaper's Washington bureau. U.N. officials declined to give further details of the device because of an ongoing investigation. But other sources said that, like those received in Washington, they bore an Alexandria, Egypt, postmark.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters as he left the building, "We consider it an attack on the organisation and also on freedom of press and speech. We hope that whoever has undertaken this cowardly act will cease before some serious damage is done."

"This is a house of peace and we work in the interest of all nations," he said, adding: This kind of activity is not something that anyone can condone and I appeal to them to desist and use other means to raise their complaints."
The FBI launched an investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.
Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.

Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as are Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters and other targets.
